paras.text: Sitework, Concrete, and Foundations, Audio Lecture

This is the biggest block on your trade exam. Excavation and sitework, site engineering, concrete, and footings and foundations together are thirty two of the one hundred ten trade questions. Almost one in three.

Everything here comes from the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code, chapter four, plus the MISS DIG law and the MIOSHA excavation rules. The exam is closed book, so these numbers have to be in your head, not in a table you know how to find.

We are going to walk it in the order a real job happens. Engineer the site. Dig. Form and pour. Then keep water out of the basement. That order is doing work for you, because the numbers stop being a list and start being a sequence you have lived.
And I will tell you now what the single most important number in this chapter is, so you are listening for it. Forty two inches. We will get there.
Idea one. Reading the site, and two words people mix up.
Before anyone digs you read the plot plan. It shows property lines, setbacks, easements, the building footprint, utilities, well and septic, and contour lines.
Two definitions the exam loves, and they are easy to keep straight if you attach each one to a direction.
A benchmark is a permanent point of known elevation. That is vertical control, your starting point for every height measurement on the job.
A monument is a permanent marker of a property corner or boundary. That is horizontal control, and disturbing one is illegal.
Benchmark, height. Monument, boundary.
Contour lines connect points of equal elevation. Close together means steep, far apart means flat, and contour lines never cross.
Now the leveling math, because they will make you do it, and it is only two sentences of arithmetic.
Height of instrument equals the benchmark elevation plus the backsight reading. Then any point's elevation equals the height of instrument minus the foresight reading at that point.

Work one with me. Benchmark is one hundred point zero. You shoot it and the backsight reads four and a half feet. So the height of instrument is one hundred four and a half. Now you shoot the garage corner and the foresight reads six and a quarter. One hundred four and a half minus six and a quarter is ninety eight and a quarter. That corner sits at ninety eight and a quarter.
And carry this logic check, because it catches sign errors. A higher rod reading means lower ground. If the rod reads big, you are standing in a hole.
Idea two. Wells and septic, for rural sites.

A percolation test measures how fast water drains through the soil, in minutes per inch, and it sizes the septic drain field. Too slow, think dense clay, slower than about sixty minutes per inch, and it fails.
The numbers, and I will tell you which are state code and which are local practice, because that distinction is itself testable.
A one thousand gallon tank is the minimum regardless of flow, and that one is in the state E G L E criteria. Twelve fifty for four bedrooms is common local practice.

The state well code minimum is fifty feet from a single family well to both the septic tank and the drain field. Many local health departments push the drain field out to seventy five or one hundred feet. Tank ten feet from the foundation and drain field twenty feet are local practice numbers.
The well casing runs at least twenty five feet below grade and sticks up twelve inches above grade. That is state well code, rule R three twenty five point sixteen thirty two.
Idea three. MISS DIG, and the trap about what is actually the crime.
Before a single bucket of dirt moves in Michigan you call MISS DIG. Dial eight one one at least three full working days before excavating.
Working days. Not calendar days, and not seventy two hours. That is Public Act one seventy four of twenty thirteen.

Now the part the exam tests. Failing to call gets you a civil fine of up to five thousand dollars. But knowingly damaging or hiding utility marks is the misdemeanor. So if a question asks which conduct is criminal, it is not the failure to call, it is destroying or concealing the marks.

And one more limit that matters on real jobs. MISS DIG only marks member utility lines. The homeowner's private lines, the feed to the detached garage, the line to the well, are on you. Hitting the homeowner's private line is your problem, and the ticket says you called.
Know the colors. Red is electric. Yellow is gas or oil. Orange is telecom. Blue is water. Green is sewer. White is your own proposed dig. Pink is survey. Purple is reclaimed water.
Question. You call MISS DIG on Monday morning. When can you dig, and what is the criminal offense in this whole area of law.
Three full working days later, so not before Thursday, and weekends and holidays do not count. And the misdemeanor is knowingly damaging or hiding the marks, not failing to call.
Idea four. Trench numbers, which are four numbers in one ladder.
At four feet deep you need a ladder or ramp within twenty five feet of lateral travel.
At five feet deep you need a protective system. Sloping, benching, shoring, or a trench box. Unless you are in stable rock.
At twenty feet deep the protective system must be designed by a registered professional engineer.
And the spoil pile and equipment stay at least two feet back from the edge.
Four, five, twenty, two. Ladder, protection, engineer, setback.

Then the contrast that catches everyone. Six feet is the fall protection trigger. Five feet is the trench trigger. Different rules, different numbers, and the exam will put them in the same question to see if you blend them.
Soil types again, and you met these in the safety chapter, so this is your second pass.

Stable rock can stand vertical. Type A is stiff clay, one and a half tons per square foot or more, sloped three quarters to one, fifty three degrees. Type B is the medium soils, one to one, forty five degrees. Type C is sand, gravel, or anything submerged or seeping, one and a half to one, thirty four degrees.
The weaker the soil, the flatter the slope.
And here is the Type C trap that is specific to this chapter. You can never bench Type C soil. Benching is for A and B only. Type C gets sloped or boxed, never stepped.
Every excavation needs a competent person, somebody who can identify hazards and has the authority to fix them, inspecting daily and after every rain.
Idea five. Two Michigan permits people confuse.

A soil erosion and sedimentation control permit, Part ninety one of the natural resources act, is triggered by disturbing one acre or more, or by any earth change within five hundred feet of a lake or stream.
Wetlands are a completely different program, Part three oh three.
So if the question says wetland, the answer is not Part ninety one. One acre or five hundred feet of water is Part ninety one. Wetland is Part three oh three.
Idea six. What the footing sits on.
Footings sit on undisturbed natural soil or engineered fill. Never on organic muck, never on loose fill, and never on frozen ground.

Presumptive bearing values, worst to best, and hear the ladder. Clay and silt, fifteen hundred pounds per square foot. Sand, two thousand. Sandy gravel, three thousand. Sedimentary rock, four thousand. Crystalline bedrock, twelve thousand.
Compaction gets verified against a Proctor test. The lab finds the soil's maximum dry density, and the field spec is usually ninety to ninety five percent of it.
Idea seven. Forty two inches, and the footing itself.
Here is the number I promised you. All exterior footings and foundation systems extend forty two inches below actual grade. That is Michigan frost depth.

And it is a Michigan amendment, which is exactly why it is worth a question. The generic I R C answer of twelve inches below grade is a trap on this exam. If you have studied from a national book, that book is wrong for Michigan. Forty two.

There are exemptions. Freestanding accessory buildings up to six hundred square feet of light frame construction, or four hundred square feet of heavier construction, with eaves ten feet or less. And freestanding decks not attached to the house.
Now footing dimensions.

Minimum thickness is six inches. The footing projects at least two inches beyond each face of the wall, and here is the rule that goes with it, that projection can never exceed the footing's own thickness. So a six inch footing can project up to six inches, and no more.
Width comes from the code tables based on soil strength and the number of stories. Twelve inches is the everyday light frame answer on decent soil, and it widens as the soil weakens.
The top of a footing must be level. The bottom can slope up to one in ten, which is ten percent. Steeper than that and you step the footing.
And building next to a slope steeper than one vertical in three horizontal, which is thirty three percent, triggers special setback rules.
Question. Michigan frost depth for exterior footings, and what is the limit on how far a footing projects past the wall.
Forty two inches below actual grade. And the projection is at least two inches but never more than the thickness of the footing itself.
Idea eight. Anchor bolts, which is one string you should be able to say in one breath.

Half inch diameter minimum. Six feet on center maximum. Seven inches embedded into the concrete or grouted block. At least two bolts per plate section. One within twelve inches of each end. Sitting in the middle third of the plate width. Nut and washer tightened.
Say that again on your own after this. Half inch, six feet, seven inches, two per plate, twelve inches from each end.

Now disarm the trap. You may have read that buildings over two stories need four foot spacing. That is a seismic rule, for seismic design categories C and D. Michigan is category A or B. So six feet on center governs here no matter how many stories.
Same reason you do not need the big three by three plate washers. That is earthquake country equipment, not Michigan equipment.
Idea nine. Foundation walls and backfill.
Wall thickness comes from tables driven by three things, wall height, unbalanced backfill height, and soil class.
The wall must stick up above finished grade at least four inches where masonry veneer is used, and six inches everywhere else. Four with veneer, six without.

And the backfill rule, which is a real world rule as much as an exam rule. Never backfill until the wall has cured and is braced or anchored to the floor framing above. Then backfill in six to twelve inch compacted lifts of clean material. A green wall with a dozer pushing against it is how basement walls crack before the house is even framed.
Idea ten. Keeping the basement dry, which is three separate systems.
The exam tests whether you can tell these three apart, so name them as you learn them.
System one is surface grading. The ground falls six inches in the first ten feet away from the foundation. Impervious surfaces need two percent.
System two is foundation drains. Drain tile or perforated pipe at or below the top of the footing, discharging by gravity or pump to an approved outlet.

The gravel geometry around that pipe gets tested, so hear it precisely. The gravel extends one full foot beyond the outside edge of the footing, and six inches above the top of the footing, wrapped in filter fabric. The pipe sits on two inches of washed gravel with six inches over it.
And there is an exemption. No drain is needed on well drained gravelly Group One soils.

System three is the wall coating, and this is the discrimination question. Dampproofing is the default. It runs from the top of the footing to finished grade, a bituminous coating, and masonry walls get parged first with three eighths of an inch of portland cement.
Waterproofing, meaning an actual membrane, is required only where a high water table or severe soil water conditions are known.
Here is the one line that answers every question about the pair. Dampproofing stops soil moisture. Waterproofing stops water under pressure.
Question. Name the three systems that keep a basement dry, and tell me which wall coating is the default.

Surface grading at six inches in ten feet, foundation drains at or below the top of the footing, and the wall coating. Dampproofing is the default. Waterproofing only where a high water table or severe soil water conditions are known.
Idea eleven. Crawl spaces, which is four numbers.

Vent area is one square foot of vent per one hundred fifty square feet of floor. That drops to one per fifteen hundred if you have a ground vapor retarder, and you need a vent within three feet of each corner.
Access sizes. Through the floor, eighteen by twenty four inches. Through a perimeter wall, sixteen by twenty four.
Hook for that pair. Floor is bigger, eighteen. Wall is sixteen.
Idea twelve. Concrete strength, and why Michigan is different.
All of Michigan is severe weathering. That single fact drives the strength table, so learn three numbers.
Twenty five hundred p s i for footings, interior slabs, and foundation walls not exposed to weather.
Three thousand for vertical concrete exposed to weather.
Thirty five hundred for garage floor slabs, porches, carport slabs, and steps. Anything that is going to see deicing salt off a truck or a boot.

And every piece of exterior concrete gets air entrainment, five to seven percent. Those microscopic bubbles give freezing water somewhere to expand into, which is the whole reason concrete survives a Michigan winter.

Mix basics. Water cement ratio runs around point four five to point five zero. And know the consequence of the site request you get on every pour, adding water on site raises the slump but kills strength.
A slump test measures workability. Four to six inches is normal residential, and footings are often two to four.

Admixtures, four types by job. Accelerators for cold weather, but never calcium chloride around embedded or prestressed steel, because chlorides corrode it. Retarders for hot weather and long hauls. Water reducers when you want workability without adding water. Air entrainers for freeze and thaw.
Idea thirteen. Where the steel goes, which is a classic discrimination question.
Footing rebar goes in the bottom third, because that is the tension zone, with three inches of cover where concrete is cast against earth.
Welded wire mesh in a slab goes in the upper third, on chairs. Mesh lying in the dirt does nothing at all. It is not a little less effective, it is useless.
Bottom third for footing rebar, upper third for slab mesh.
Bar sizes are eighths of an inch. Number three is three eighths. Number four is a half inch. Number five is five eighths.
Idea fourteen. Finishing, in order, because the order is the answer.
Screed. Bull float. Then stop.
That stop is the tested part. You let the bleed water evaporate, and you never finish bleed water back into the surface. Working that water back in is what gives you a dusting, scaling slab.
Then edge, cut your joints, float, and trowel. Trowel interior only, because a steel trowel makes exterior concrete dangerously slick. Outside gets a broom finish for traction.

Three joints, three jobs. Control joints get cut at least a quarter of the slab depth, spaced roughly eight to twelve feet on a four inch slab. Isolation joints separate the slab from walls and columns. Construction joints end a day's pour.
Idea fifteen. Curing and cold weather.
Concrete reaches about seventy percent of design strength at seven days, and full design strength at twenty eight days. Keep it moist and around fifty degrees.
In cold weather, never pour on frozen ground. And protect fresh concrete from freezing until it reaches five hundred p s i, which is roughly the first forty eight to seventy two hours.
Interior slabs are three and a half inches thick minimum, over four inches of granular base, over six mil poly.
And the volume math, same as the estimating chapter. Length times width times thickness, all in feet, divided by twenty seven gives cubic yards. Then order ten percent extra.
Question. Garage floor slab in Michigan. What strength, what air content, and what finish.
Thirty five hundred p s i because it sees deicing salt, five to seven percent air entrainment because it is exterior exposure, and a broom finish for traction, never a steel trowel.
Rapid fire recap. Say these with me.

Forty two inches, Michigan frost depth. Six in ten, grade away from the house. Six inches footing thickness, two inches footing projection, never more than the thickness. Half inch, six feet, seven inches, two per plate, twelve from the end, anchor bolts. Four with veneer, six otherwise, wall above grade. One foot beyond and six inches above, drain gravel. Twenty five hundred, three thousand, thirty five hundred, footings, exposed walls, garage slabs. Five to seven percent air. Four to six slump. Seven days seventy percent, twenty eight days full strength. Fifty degrees and five hundred p s i for cold weather. Three and a half inch slab, four inch base, six mil poly. One fifty crawl venting, eighteen by twenty four floor access, sixteen by twenty four wall access. Fifteen hundred, two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, twelve thousand, clay, sand, gravel, sedimentary rock, bedrock. Eight one one, three working days, five thousand dollar fine. Four feet ladder, five feet protection, two feet spoil, twenty feet engineer. Fifty three, forty five, thirty four degrees for A, B, and C, and you never bench Type C. One acre or five hundred feet of water, erosion permit. Fifty feet tank to well. One thousand gallons for three bedrooms.

Thirty two questions live in this chapter. If you own forty two inches, the anchor bolt string, the three concrete strengths, and the trench ladder of four, five, twenty, you have most of it. Go drill those four things.
